tldr: A definitive tutorial systematically organizing the exact formulations, convex relaxations, and numerical solvers for cone complementarity-based contact dynamics used in robotics simulators like MuJoCo and Drake, with unified notation and optimization theory.
overview:
When simulating how robots interact with their environment, computing contact dynamics is the most fundamental and computationally demanding bottleneck. Physically, contact serves two purposes: preventing penetration and dissipating energy through friction. Complementarity conditions—combining inequalities with orthogonality conditions—provide the mathematical framework to model these behaviors without prescribing contact modes (separation, sticking, or sliding) in advance.

However, existing literature has mostly targeted computational mechanics or computer graphics. There has been no comprehensive, self-contained educational resource with unified notation tailored for robotics. In particular, the mathematical distinctions between exact friction models (non-convex problems) and the convex relaxations adopted by modern simulators—as well as the resulting physical artifacts, such as lift-off during sliding and creeping under sticking contact—have not been well understood by practitioners and researchers.

This paper bridges rigid-body dynamics and conic optimization. It provides complete derivations ranging from the Signorini–Coulomb conditions to nonlinear cone complementarity problems (N-CCPs), coupled/cascaded QPs, convex relaxations (L-CCPs, QCQPs), and the nonlinear least-squares (NLS) formulations used in MuJoCo and Drake. Furthermore, it thoroughly compares the computational cost and robustness of first-order methods (PGS, PGD, ADMM), Newton-based methods, and proximal regularizations, offering a clear roadmap extending to trajectory optimization and differentiable simulation.
contributions: Derives and systematically organizes all mathematical representations of contact dynamics—from Signorini–Coulomb conditions to N-CCPs, coupled QPs, convex relaxations, and NLS formulations—using unified notation.
Clarifies the mathematical mechanisms behind the physical artifacts introduced by convex relaxations and regularizations (e.g., lift-off during sliding and creep caused by loss of static friction).
Comprehensively compares and classifies the formulations and solvers adopted by major simulators (MuJoCo, Drake, PhysX, Bullet, Kamino, Simple, etc.) along with their trade-offs.
Presents a unified proximal minimization framework that recovers exact friction solutions while internally leveraging efficient convex relaxation solvers.

sections.heading: What is a contact model? Why cone complementarity?
sections.summary: This section explains how microscopic contact phenomena are abstracted into two macroscopic functions (non-penetration and energy dissipation), the significance of cone complementarity in describing them, and the scope of this tutorial. It also clarifies the difference between existing literature in computer graphics/computational mechanics and the requirements of robotics.
sections.details:
Simulating contact forces directly from interatomic forces or the deformation of microscopic surface asperities is computationally intractable at robotic scales. Robotics therefore adopts phenomenological models that capture macroscopic behaviors: (1) preventing bodies from interpenetrating, and (2) dissipating energy along sliding surfaces. Cone complementarity elegantly casts these two effects into mathematical optimization.

### 1.1 Scope and Positioning of This Tutorial
Existing surveys primarily focus on computer graphics (collision detection, penalty methods, LCPs) or computational mechanics (rigorous theory, non-smooth mechanics). None provide a comprehensive pedagogical reference covering the convex relaxations, regularizations, and solvers routinely employed in modern robotics simulators (e.g., MuJoCo, Drake, Simple, Kamino). This tutorial focuses on impulse-based, discrete time-stepping methods and excludes event-driven schemes, continuous-time theory, and penalty methods, thereby diving deep into the most practical domain for robotics.

### 1.2 Structure of This Document
The tutorial is organized pedagogically rather than historically. It begins with the fundamentals of rigid-body dynamics and conic optimization, proceeds through problem formulations, numerical solvers, and comparative analyses, and builds up to advanced applications such as trajectory optimization and differentiable simulation.

sections.heading: Building the foundation of rigid-body simulation: Dynamics and collision detection
sections.summary: This section reviews contact-independent rigid-body dynamics (Newton-Euler equations, symplectic Euler discretization, Delassus matrix) and collision detection fundamentals that serve as inputs to contact computations. It highlights the crucial distinction between geometric time derivatives and kinematic Jacobians.
sections.details:
Simulators generally operate with three routines: rigid-body dynamics, collision detection, and contact dynamics. Contact dynamics utilizes the outputs of the first two routines to compute contact forces and the resulting motion.

### 2.1 Rigid-Body Dynamics (Continuous and Discrete Time)
The unconstrained equations of motion for generalized coordinates $q \in \mathbb{R}^{n_v}$ are written as $M(q)\ddot{q} + b(q,\dot{q}) = u$, using the generalized mass matrix $M(q)$ and bias forces $b(q, \dot{q})$ (centrifugal, Coriolis, gravity, etc.). When $N$ external contact forces $f \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}$ act through a kinematic Jacobian $J \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times n_v}$, the system becomes $M\ddot{q} + b = u + J^\top f$.
Discretizing this with the symplectic Euler scheme (time step $\Delta t$), the contact-point velocities at the end of the step $v^+ \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}$ are expressed via the unconstrained free velocity $v_f$ and the contact impulse $f \Delta t$ as $v^+ = v_f + G f \Delta t$. Here, $G = J M^{-1} J^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times 3N}$ is known as the Delassus matrix. It represents the inverse inertia projected into the contact space and plays a central role in contact dynamics computations.

### 2.2 Collision Detection and Subtleties in Derivatives
The collision detection routine outputs the signed distance $d_i$ for proximal rigid body pairs, contact witness points, surface normals $\hat{n}_i$, and contact Jacobians $J_i = J_1 - J_2$. A critical pitfall here is confusing the geometric time derivative with the kinematic Jacobian. The velocity given by the Jacobian, $J_1 \dot{q}$, is the velocity measured by an observer fixed to the rigid body. This differs from the velocity $\dot{p}_1$ of the contact point itself (defined as the point of maximum penetration) by a term related to surface curvature. While this discrepancy poses no issue in forward simulation, it becomes vital when treating contact points as decision variables in trajectory optimization.

sections.heading: Geometry of conic optimization: Why are contact forces cones?
sections.summary: This section explains the geometric properties of the second-order cone formed by normal non-negativity and Coulomb's friction law, along with dual cones, polar cones, and Moreau's decomposition theorem. It also derives complementarity functions (such as the Fischer–Burmeister function) that reformulate complementarity conditions as systems of equations.
sections.details:
Contact forces possess a distinct geometric structure. Normal forces can only push and cannot pull ($f_n \ge 0$), and tangential friction forces are bounded proportionally to the normal force by Coulomb's law ($\|f_t\| \le \mu f_n$). In three-dimensional space, this forms a circular cone (second-order cone).

### 3.1 Convex Cones and Optimality Conditions
For a convex cone $\mathcal{K}$, the set of vectors whose inner product with all elements in $\mathcal{K}$ is non-negative is called the dual cone $\mathcal{K}^*$, while the set yielding non-positive inner products is the polar cone $\mathcal{K}^\circ = -\mathcal{K}^*$. According to Moreau's decomposition theorem, any vector $x$ can be decomposed orthogonally as $x = \Pi_{\mathcal{K}}(x) + \Pi_{\mathcal{K}^\circ}(x)$. The KKT conditions for a convex program with conic constraints $\min f(x) \text{ s.t. } g(x) \in \mathcal{K}$, with Lagrange multiplier $s \in \mathcal{K}^*$, are elegantly stated as $g(x) \in \mathcal{K}$, multiplier $s \in \mathcal{K}^*$, and the complementarity condition $s^\top g(x) = 0$ (collectively written as $\mathcal{K} \ni g(x) \perp s \in \mathcal{K}^*$).

### 3.2 Isotropic Friction and 3D Cone Projections
For the Coulomb friction cone $\mathcal{K} = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \|x_t\| \le \mu x_n\}$, the projection operator $\Pi_{\mathcal{K}}$ and its Jacobian $\partial \Pi_{\mathcal{K}}$ can be computed in closed form based on the geometric relationship between the normal and tangential components.

### 3.4 Equation Reformulation via Complementarity Functions
The complementarity condition $0 \le x \perp y \ge 0$ can be rewritten as an equality constraint using a complementarity function such as the Fischer–Burmeister (FB) function $\psi(x,y) = x + y - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 0$. Extending this to second-order cones (Lorentz cones) yields the SOCFB function via the Jordan product. Introducing a smoothing parameter $\epsilon$ allows standard root-finding algorithms like Newton's method and automatic differentiation to be applied directly.

sections.heading: Mathematical models of contact: From exact transcriptions to practical convex relaxations
sections.summary: Starting from the Signorini–Coulomb conditions, this section presents exact transcriptions such as N-CCPs and coupled QPs. It then derives convex relaxations (L-CCP, QCQP) that omit the de Saxcé correction for speed, as well as the complete equivalence to the acceleration-space nonlinear least-squares (NLS) formulation used in MuJoCo and Drake.
sections.details:
Discretized contact dynamics problems fall into two categories: exact transcriptions, which preserve exact physical laws, and convex relaxations, which modify these laws for computational tractability.

### 4.1 Exact Transcriptions
- **Signorini–Coulomb Formulation**: The baseline formulation combines Signorini's non-penetration condition ($0 \le d/\Delta t + v_n^+ \perp f_n \ge 0$) directly with Coulomb friction based on the principle of maximum dissipation. In practical simulators, to prevent numerical chatter, $d/\Delta t$ is replaced by a stabilization term $\gamma_n$ analogous to Baumgarte stabilization (e.g., spring-damper terms in Kamino or MuJoCo).
- **N-CCP Formulation**: By introducing the de Saxcé correction term $\Gamma(v^+) = \mu \|v_t^+\| \hat{n}$, multiple contact conditions collapse into a single nonlinear cone complementarity problem: $\mathcal{K} \ni f \perp (v^+ + \Gamma(v^+) + \gamma) \in \mathcal{K}^*$. This correction term plays a crucial role in preventing artificial normal separation (dilatancy or lift-off) during sliding contact.
- **Root-Finding Formulation**: Transforms the N-CCP into a system of equations $\psi(f, v^+)=0$ using the SOCFB function.
- **C-QCQP and C-QP Formulations**: Formulates the exact problem as cascaded quadratically constrained quadratic programs (C-QCQP) or as two coupled bounded QPs (C-QP) where bounds on normal and tangential forces depend on each other.

### 4.2 Convex Relaxations
All exact transcriptions are non-convex problems with no known polynomial-time algorithms. Consequently, many modern simulators relax the problem into a linear cone complementarity problem (L-CCP) or a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) by omitting the de Saxcé correction $\Gamma(v^+)$. Furthermore, to prevent rank deficiency in the Delassus matrix $G$ caused by redundant contacts, a regularization matrix $R \succ 0$ is added to enforce strong convexity ($G + R \succ 0$).
- **NLS (Nonlinear Least-Squares) Formulation**: Taking the dual of the regularized QCQP yields an equivalent unconstrained, strongly convex minimization over generalized accelerations $\ddot{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_v}$ rather than contact forces $f \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}$: $\min_{\ddot{q}} \frac{1}{2}\|\ddot{q} - \ddot{q}_f\|_M^2 + \frac{1}{2}\|\Pi_\mathcal{K}(a_{\text{ref}} - J\ddot{q})\|_{R^{-1}}^2$. When the degrees of freedom $n_v$ are smaller than the contact force dimensions $3N$ (contact-rich scenarios such as multi-legged robots or multi-fingered hands), this formulation can be solved exceptionally fast. It serves as the default solver in MuJoCo and the SAP solver in Drake.

### 4.3 Physical Interpretation of Convex Relaxations
Inspecting the optimality conditions of the NLS formulation reveals that it corresponds exactly to contact forces acting in inverse dynamics as $f_i = R_{ii}^{-1} \Pi_{\mathcal{K}}(a_{\text{ref}} - J\ddot{q})$. Moreover, in the ideal case without penalty terms, contact dynamics follows the physical principle of minimizing the total kinetic energy at the end of the time step: $\frac{1}{2}(\dot{q}^+)^\top M \dot{q}^+$.

sections.heading: The landscape of numerical solvers: First-order, Newton, and proximal methods
sections.summary: This section details various algorithms for solving formulated contact problems. It covers PGS, PGD, ADMM, interior-point methods, and acceleration-space Newton methods, along with the proximal minimization framework (used in Simple and Kamino) that converges to exact solutions while driving convex solvers under the hood.
sections.details:
Algorithms are broadly divided into those solving convex relaxations and those solving exact formulations.

### 5.1 Solvers for Convex Relaxations
- **Projected Gauss–Seidel (PGS)**: Converts complementarity conditions into fixed-point equations $x = \Pi_\mathcal{K}(x - \rho F(x))$ and sequentially updates contact forces by projecting onto the cone one contact at a time. It requires no linear system factorizations and is easy to implement and robust, but convergence is very slow on ill-conditioned problems with high mass ratios or dense contacts.
- **Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)**: Performs gradient descent on all contact forces simultaneously before projecting. It is well suited for parallel computing.
- **ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers)**: Introduces an auxiliary equality constraint $\hat{f} = f$ on contact forces, alternating between solving a linear system (factored only once initially) and cone projections. It is far more robust to ill-conditioning than PGS and forms the backbone of Simple and Kamino.
- **Interior-Point Methods**: Solve the problem using Newton steps with logarithmic barrier terms. They achieve high accuracy in very few iterations, but require refactoring matrices at every step.
- **Newton's Method on NLS (Todorov's Solver)**: Because the decision variables are generalized accelerations $\ddot{q}$, the linear system size is only $n_v \times n_v$. It runs extremely fast by exploiting sparsity in the inertia matrix $M$ (the default in MuJoCo).

### 5.2 Solvers for Exact Formulations and Proximal Methods
- **Gauss–Seidel with Local Exact Solutions (Moreau–Jean)**: Solves the discrete three-way branching (separation, sticking, sliding) per contact while holding all others fixed, as implemented in Siconos.
- **Non-smooth Newton Methods (Alart–Curnier / Fischer–Burmeister)**: Solve residual equations for all contacts simultaneously via Newton steps. They offer superlinear convergence, but only hold local convergence guarantees and can fail if $G$ loses rank, requiring fallbacks to PGS.
- **Proximal Minimization with de Saxcé Correction (Algorithm 14)**: A powerful framework combining the strengths of convex solvers (global convergence, speed) with the physical fidelity of exact formulations. The outer loop updates a proximal penalty $\frac{\rho}{2}\|f - z\|^2$ toward the previous iterate $z$ along with the de Saxcé correction term. The inner loop solves a regularized convex relaxation (such as a QCQP) using any solver (e.g., ADMM). At convergence, the proximal penalty vanishes, matching the exact N-CCP solution precisely.

sections.heading: In-depth comparison: Solution existence, uniqueness, and physical reality trade-offs
sections.summary: This section mathematically compares the solution properties (existence and uniqueness) of exact formulations versus convex relaxations, and explains physical artifacts introduced by convex relaxations, such as lift-off and creeping (loss of stiction). It also summarizes CPU/GPU implementation perspectives and practical selection guidelines.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Existence and Uniqueness of Solutions
In exact formulations, solutions may not exist in situations like physically wedged geometries. Furthermore, due to contact redundancy or Coulomb friction properties (Painlevé's paradox), multiple contact force distributions may correspond to the same motion, or the motion itself may be non-unique. When multiple solutions exist, solver details—such as PGS update ordering, initial guesses, or the central path in interior-point methods—arbitrarily select which solution is returned.
In contrast, regularized convex relaxations (strongly convex problems) always guarantee a mathematically unique solution, distributing redundant contact forces smoothly via norm minimization.

### 6.2 Physical Artifacts Introduced by Convex Relaxations
Relaxations introduced for computational ease create unphysical behaviors:
- **Lift-off phenomenon**: Dropping the de Saxcé correction forces the normal velocity during sliding contact to satisfy $v_n^+ + \gamma_n = \mu \|v_t^+\|$. As a result, sliding an object horizontally across a table causes it to levitate into the air at a rate proportional to its sliding velocity and friction coefficient.
- **Loss of static friction and creeping**: Adding the regularization term $f^\top R f$ biases contact forces toward zero. As shown by inverse dynamics, zero velocity and acceleration ($\dot{q}=0, \ddot{q}=0$) cannot generate tangential contact forces. Consequently, no matter how hard two fingers pinch an object against gravity, the object inevitably creeps downward.

### 6.3 Guidelines for Solvers and Hardware (CPU vs. GPU)
- **Reinforcement Learning / Massive Parallelization (Throughput-oriented)**: If minor artifacts are tolerable, NLS formulations solved with Newton's method (MuJoCo/MJX) or GPU-friendly PGS/TGS (PhysX) are ideal due to guaranteed uniqueness and high speed.
- **Manipulation / Grasping (Fidelity-oriented)**: Grasping tasks where static friction is vital will fail under convex relaxations. Solvers must target exact friction laws using proximal ADMM (Simple, Kamino), exact Newton methods, or coupled bounded QPs.
- **Differentiability (Trajectory Optimization / System ID)**: Root-finding Newton methods with smoothed SOCFB functions or interior-point methods with log-barriers provide smooth gradients.

sections.heading: Beyond forward simulation: Optimal control and differentiable simulation
sections.summary: This section reviews cutting-edge developments in integrating contact models into trajectory optimization (MPCC, contact-implicit MPC) and differentiable simulation. It discusses overcoming non-smooth collision detection, dynamics gradients, zero gradients in non-contact states, and time-discretization sensitivity errors.
sections.details:
The value of contact models extends beyond advancing time in forward simulation. Their true utility emerges in planning motions that deliberately establish or break contact (trajectory optimization) and in learning physical parameters from data via differentiable simulation.

### 7.1 Contact Models in Planning and Optimal Control
Trajectory optimization subject to complementarity constraints is known as a Mathematical Program with Complementarity Constraints (MPCC). These problems are notoriously difficult because they violate standard constraint qualifications (CQs). Approaches to solving them include direct methods that treat contact conditions directly as constraints (e.g., Consensus Complementarity Control ($C^3$) and NOSBENCH) and bi-level methods that invoke a forward simulator as an inner optimization problem.

### 7.2 Four Major Challenges in Differentiable Simulation
Propagating gradients through a simulator via backpropagation involves specific hurdles:
1. **Differentiating collision detection**: While smooth convex primitives (such as spheres) yield smooth derivatives, contact witness points between polygonal meshes jump discontinuously at vertices and edges. Current research explores randomized smoothing, implicit differentiation via the Implicit Function Theorem, and smooth proximity distance approximations.
2. **Differentiating contact dynamics**: Complementarity mode switching introduces derivative discontinuities. Implicit differentiation via interior-point methods or smoothed FB functions, as well as solver unrolling with automatic differentiation, are used. Care must be taken regarding gradient bias across non-smooth boundaries.
3. **Vanishing gradients in non-contact regimes**: When a robot's hand is slightly separated from an object, the gradient is strictly zero, preventing gradient-based discovery of contact. Addressing this involves log-barriers or relaxed $\gamma$ terms that exert soft forces at a distance to supply informative gradients, or relaxing constraints only during optimization (e.g., DiffContact).
4. **Pathologies of time discretization**: In non-smooth systems with Coulomb friction, reducing the time step does not necessarily converge to correct continuous-time sensitivities. Advanced integrators such as Finite Elements on Switching Grids (FESD/FESD-J) are being developed to explicitly capture mode transition boundaries.

sections.heading: Summary: Foundational insights for selecting and building contact models
sections.summary: This section summarizes the fundamental trade-off between exact formulations (non-convex, high fidelity) and regularized convex relaxations (strongly convex, fast, artifact-prone), providing a perspective to help readers select and develop optimal models and solvers for their research.
sections.details:
Starting from the two core functions of contact mechanics (non-penetration and energy dissipation) and bridging rigid-body dynamics with conic optimization, this tutorial has systematically organized complementarity-based contact models powering modern robotics simulators.

The fundamental takeaway is the inherent trade-off: pursuing the exact Signorini–Coulomb law yields non-convex problems that are challenging to solve, whereas introducing convex relaxations and regularization for computational efficiency and solution uniqueness inevitably produces physical artifacts such as lift-off and loss of static friction (creep). The proximal minimization framework (Algorithm 14) serves as a promising bridge, reaching exact solutions while reaping the benefits of convex relaxation solvers.

Equipped with the concepts in this paper, researchers can accurately understand the internal mechanics of simulators like MuJoCo, Drake, PhysX, and Kamino, diagnose simulation artifacts, and confidently pursue advanced research in contact-implicit trajectory optimization and differentiable simulation.

takeaways: Convex relaxations adopted by fast simulators like MuJoCo and Drake fundamentally suffer from physical artifacts—such as lift-off during sliding and creeping due to the loss of static friction—as a direct trade-off for computational stability.

In contact-rich environments where contact dimensions $3N$ exceed degrees of freedom $n_v$, solving in generalized acceleration space via the NLS formulation (Todorov's approach) is computationally superior to solving in contact force space.

When high physical fidelity is required (e.g., sticking friction in grasping), proximal methods that run a convex relaxation in an inner loop while updating the de Saxcé correction in an outer loop offer the most practical solution.

When implementing differentiable simulation or contact trajectory optimization, practitioners should account for zero gradients in non-contact states and geometric discontinuities in polygonal contact, and consider using interior-point methods or smoothed complementarity functions (SOCFB).
limitations: This tutorial focuses strictly on rigid-body impulse theory (discrete time-stepping) and explicitly excludes continuous contact models such as large-deformation soft body contact or hydroelastic pressure field models.
While geometric errors in collision detection and mesh artifact issues at corners are discussed, fast and robust geometric computation algorithms themselves fall outside the scope.
There remains no general-purpose solver capable of guaranteeing a global optimum in polynomial time for the exact non-convex Coulomb friction problem.
